'''Armand Paul Alivisatos''' (born November 12, 1959) is an American chemist who has been the [[President of the University of Chicago|14th president]] of the [[University of Chicago]] since September 2021.

Previously at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], he served as the 7th director of [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] from 2009 to 2016, as interim vice chancellor for research from 2016 to 2017, and as executive vice chancellor and provost from 2017 to 2021.

His academic research focuses on [[nanomaterials]],<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal |last1=Wilson |first1=E. |date=February 8, 2010 |title=Paul Alivisatos: LBNL's new director focuses on renewable energy, climate |journal=Chemical and Engineering News |volume=88 |issue=6 |page=55 |doi=10.1021/cen-v088n006.p055}}</ref><ref name="National Award Recipient Citations">{{cite web |title=National Award Recipient Citations |url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/2014-recipient-citations.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140903041600/http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/2014-recipient-citations.html |archive-date=September 3, 2014 |access-date=June 9, 2014 |website=www.acs.org |publisher=American Chemical Society}}</ref> particularly nanocrystal fabrication for biomedical and renewable energy applications.<ref>{{cite news |date=May 30, 2014 |title=Paul Alivisatos: Berkeley Lab director navigates uncertain times with a focus on research |url=http://spie.org/x108554.xml |access-date=June 11, 2014 |publisher=SPIE: The International Society for Optics & Photonics |issue=DOI: 10.1117/2.321405.05 |agency=SPIE Newsroom}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Paul Alivisatos was born in [[Chicago]], Illinois,<ref name="ReferenceA" /> where he lived until the age of 10, when his family moved to [[Athens]], [[Greece]]. He returned to the United States to attend the University of Chicago in the late 1970s.<ref>{{cite web|title=Lawrence Berkeley National Lab: Leadership: Berkeley Lab Director Paul Alivisatos|url=http://www.lbl.gov/lab-leadership/director/|website=www.lbl.gov|publisher=Lawrence Berkeley National Lab|access-date=June 10, 2014}}</ref>

Alivisatos received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree (with honors) with a major in chemistry from the University of Chicago in 1981 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in physical chemistry from the University of California, Berkeley, in 1986. His doctoral advisor at Berkeley was [[Charles B. Harris]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Outstanding Young Investigator Award Given to Alivisatos for Nanocrystal Research|journal=MRS Bulletin|date=Feb 1995|volume=20|issue=2|pages=63|doi=10.1557/S0883769400049277|doi-access=free}}</ref> His doctoral thesis was titled ''The photophysical properties of molecules near metal and semiconductor surfaces''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=THE PHOTOPHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF MOLECULES NEAR METAL AND SEMICONDUCTOR SURFACES - ProQuest |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/303450332 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250425070732/https://www.proquest.com/docview/303450332/ |archive-date=April 25, 2025 |access-date=August 12, 2025 |website=www.proquest.com |id={{ProQuest|303450332}} |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Career ==
After receiving his doctorate, Alivisatos joined [[American Telephone & Telegraph|AT&T]] [[Bell Labs]] working with [[Louis E. Brus]], and began research in the field of [[nanotechnology]].

=== University of California, Berkeley ===
Alivisatos returned to the University of California, Berkeley in 1988 as an assistant professor of chemistry. He was promoted to associate professor in 1993 and to full professor in 1995.{{Citation needed|date=August 2025}}

In administrative roles, Alivisatos served as the 7th director of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory from 2009 to 2016, as the university's interim vice chancellor for research from 2016 to 2017, and as executive vice chancellor and provost from 2017 to 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Srivastava |first=Ishaan |date=January 25, 2016 |title=Paul Alivisatos appointed as UC Berkeley's vice chancellor for research |url=http://www.dailycal.org/2016/01/24/paul-alivisatos-appointed-uc-berkeleys-vice-chancellor-research/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160322025203/http://www.dailycal.org/2016/01/24/paul-alivisatos-appointed-uc-berkeleys-vice-chancellor-research/ |archive-date=March 22, 2016 |access-date=September 25, 2025 |website=The Daily Californian |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=EVCP Paul Alivisatos {{!}} Executive Vice Chancellor and Provost |url=https://evcp.berkeley.edu/evcp-paul-alivisatos |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250826014552/http://evcp.berkeley.edu/evcp-paul-alivisatos |archive-date=August 26, 2025 |access-date=September 25, 2025 |website=evcp.berkeley.edu}}</ref>

In August 2013, he was appointed as Samsung Distinguished Professor in Nanoscience and Nanotechnology Research.<ref>{{cite news |date=August 22, 2013 |title=Alivisatos appointed Samsung Distinguished Chair in Nanoscience |url=http://newscenter.berkeley.edu/2013/08/22/alivisatos-appointed-samsung-distinguished-chair-in-nanoscience/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130827010932/http://newscenter.berkeley.edu/2013/08/22/alivisatos-appointed-samsung-distinguished-chair-in-nanoscience/ |archive-date=August 27, 2013 |access-date=September 2, 2014 |work= |publisher=University of California, Berkeley |agency=UC Berkeley News Center}}</ref> He was also the founding director of the Kavli Energy Nanosciences Institute (ENSI).<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brown |first1=S. |date=October 4, 2013 |title=UC Berkeley, Lawrence Berkeley Lab open new energy nanoscience center |url=http://www.bizjournals.com/sanfrancisco/news/2013/10/04/uc-berkeley-lawrence-berkeley-lab.html |access-date=June 10, 2014 |agency=SF Business Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Introducing the Kavli Energy NanoSciences Institute |url=http://www.kavlifoundation.org/science-spotlights/Kavli-ENSI-feature#.VAM8OLxdV2c |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200703103129/https://www.kavlifoundation.org/science-spotlights/Kavli-ENSI-feature#.VAM8OLxdV2c |archive-date=July 3, 2020 |access-date=June 9, 2014 |website=www.kavlifoundation.org |publisher=The Kavli Foundation}}</ref>

==== Lawrence Berkeley National Lab ====
Alivisatos joined the Materials Sciences Division at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in 1991. He served as associate laboratory director for physical sciences from 2005 to 2007. In 2008, he became deputy director, and he stepped in as interim director after [[Steven Chu]] left to become [[United States Secretary of Energy]] under the [[Presidency of Barack Obama|first Obama administration]].<ref>{{cite web |title=A. Paul Alivisatos |url=http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?alivisatosa |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140903113341/http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?alivisatosa |archive-date=September 3, 2014 |access-date=August 31, 2014 |website=www.aip.org |publisher=Array of Contemporary American Physicists}}</ref><ref name="About the Director-Berkeley Lab">{{Cite web |title=Director |url=https://www.lbl.gov/lab-leadership/director/ |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090116073002/http://www.lbl.gov/Publications/Director/ |archivedate=January 16, 2009 |website=www.lbl.gov}}</ref>

On November 19, 2009, Alivisatos was appointed 7th director of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. He refocused the lab on renewable energy and climate research, oversaw new facilities, deepened ties to the national innovation ecosystem, and advanced collaborations that sped technology transfer across industries from autos to medicine.<ref name="ReferenceA" /><ref name="National Award Recipient Citations" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Director's Q&A |url=http://diversity.lbl.gov/directors-q-a/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170701035917/http://diversity.lbl.gov/directors-q-a/ |archive-date=July 1, 2017 |access-date=July 22, 2014 |website=diversity.lbl.gov |publisher=Lawrence Berkeley National Lab}}</ref> On March 23, 2015, he announced that he would step down from the directorship once a successor was named.<ref>{{cite web |date=March 24, 2015 |title=Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory director to step down |url=http://www.dailycal.org/2015/03/23/lawrence-berkeley-national-laboratory-director-to-step-down/ |access-date=March 24, 2015 |publisher=Daily California}}</ref>

=== University of Chicago ===
On February 26, 2021, the Board of Trustees of the University of Chicago named Alivisatos as the incoming 14th president of the University of Chicago, with his term beginning on September 1, 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 26, 2021 |title=Paul Alivisatos named next president of the University of Chicago {{!}} University of Chicago News |url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/paul-alivisatos-named-next-president-university-chicago |access-date=September 25, 2025 |website=news.uchicago.edu |language=en}}</ref> He succeeded [[Robert Zimmer]], who served as the university president from July 2006 to August 2021.<ref>{{cite web |date=March 2021 |title=A greeting from incoming President Paul Alivisatos to the University community |url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/greeting-incoming-president-paul-alivisatos-university-community |access-date=September 3, 2021 |publisher=University of Chicago News}}</ref> In addition to the office of the president, he was named the John D. MacArthur Distinguished Service Professor, chair of the Board of Governors of [[Argonne National Laboratory]], and chair of the Board of Directors of Fermi Forward Discovery Group LLC, which operates the [[Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory]].<ref name="auto">{{cite web |date=September 1, 2020 |title=About President Alivisatos |url=https://president.uchicago.edu/biography/ |access-date=September 3, 2021 |publisher=University of Chicago |agency=University of Chicago Office of Communications}}</ref>

On September 24, 2025, the Board of Trustees of the University of Chicago extended Alivisatos's presidency through June 2030.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 24, 2025 |title=Paul Alivisatos's term as UChicago president extended through June 2030 {{!}} University of Chicago News |url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/paul-alivisatoss-term-uchicago-president-extended-through-june-2030 |access-date=September 25, 2025 |website=news.uchicago.edu |language=en}}</ref>

== Academic research ==
Alivisatos is an internationally recognized authority on nano chemistry in the synthesis of semiconductor quantum dots and multi-shaped artificial nanostructures.<ref name="University of California Berkeley">{{cite news|last1=Yarris|first1=L.|title=Berkeley Lab Director Paul Alivisatos Wins Wolf Prize in Chemistry|url=https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/news/berkeley-lab-director-paul-alivisatos-wins-wolf-prize-chemistry|access-date=July 22, 2014|agency=Berkeley Research University of California News|publisher=University of California Berkeley|date=January 12, 2012}}</ref> Further, he is a world expert on the chemistry of nanoscale crystals; one of his papers (Science, 271: 933–937, 1996) has been cited over 13,800 times.<ref>{{cite web|title=Science, 271: 933–937, 1996|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&q=science%2C+271%3A+933-937%2C+1996&btnG=&as_sdt=1%2C5&as_sdtp=|website=scholar.google.com|access-date=August 22, 2014}}</ref> He is also an expert on how these can be applied, for example as biological markers (e.g., Science, 281: 2013–16, 1998; a paper cited over 10,900 times<ref>{{cite web|title=Science, 281, 1998, alivisatos|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Science%2C+281%2C+1998%2C+alivisatos&btnG=&hl=en&as_sdt=0%2C5|website=scholar.google.com|access-date=August 22, 2014}}</ref>). In addition, his use of DNA in this area ([[DNA nanotechnology]]) has shown the surprising versatility of this molecule. He has used it to direct crystal growth and create new materials, as in Nature, 382: 609–11, 1996, and even to measure nanoscale distances (see Nature Nanotechnology, 1: 47–52, 2006).<ref name="DNA Nanotechnology: Chemistry">{{cite web|last1=Emsley|first1=J.|title=DNA Nanotechnology: Chemistry|url=http://sciencewatch.com/nobel/predictions/dna-nanotechnology|website=sciencewatch.com|publisher=Thomson Reuters|access-date=June 9, 2014}}</ref>

In February 2011, Alivisatos was ranked fifth among the world's top 100 chemists for the period 2000–2010 in the list released by [[Thomson Reuters]].<ref>{{cite news |date=February 10, 2011 |title=Science Watch: Top 100 Chemists, 2000–2010: Special Report on High-Impact Chemists |url=http://archive.sciencewatch.com/dr/sci/misc/Top100Chemists2000-10/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141223030922/http://archive.sciencewatch.com/dr/sci/misc/Top100Chemists2000-10/ |archive-date=December 23, 2014 |access-date=June 10, 2014 |agency=Thomson Reuters}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=February 26, 2021 |title=UChicago alumnus, distinguished leader and scientist at the University of California, Berkeley to become 14th president |url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/paul-alivisatos-named-next-president-university-chicago}}</ref>

He is widely recognized as being the first to demonstrate that semiconductor nanocrystals can be grown into complex two-dimensional shapes, as opposed to simple one-dimensional spheres.<ref name="DNA Nanotechnology: Chemistry"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Nanotechnology expert Paul Alivisatos wins Wolf Prize in Chemistry|url=http://www.nanowerk.com/news/newsid=23945.php|access-date=June 9, 2014|agency=Nanowerk News|publisher=Nanowerk|date=January 12, 2012}}</ref> Alivisatos proved that controlling the growth of nanocrystals is the key to controlling both their size and shape. This achievement altered the nanoscience landscape and paved the way for a slew of new potential applications, including biomedical diagnostics, revolutionary photovoltaic cells, and LED materials.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Bernstein|first1=M.|title=ACS Nano Letters co-editors A. Paul Alivisatos and Charles M. Lieber win prestigious Wolf Foundation Prize|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2012/january/acs-nano-letters-co-editors-a-paul-alivisatos-and-charles-m-lieber-win-prestigious-wolf-foundation-prize.html|access-date=June 9, 2014|work=press release|publisher=American Chemical Society|date=January 19, 2012}}</ref>

=== Nanocrystals ===
Nanocrystals are aggregates of anywhere from a few hundred to tens of thousands of atoms that combine into a crystalline form of matter known as a "cluster." Typically a few nanometers in diameter, nanocrystals are larger than molecules but smaller than bulk solids and therefore often exhibit physical and chemical properties somewhere in between. Given that a nanocrystal is virtually all surface and no interior, its properties can vary considerably as the crystal grows in size.

Prior to Alivisatos's research, all non-metal nanocrystals were dot-shaped, meaning they were essentially one-dimensional. No techniques had been reported for making two-dimensional or rod-shaped semiconductor nanocrystals that would also be of uniform size. However, in a landmark paper that appeared in the March 2, 2000, issue of the journal [[Nature (journal)|Nature]],<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Peng, X. G. |author2=Manna, L. |author3=Yang, W. D. |author4=Wickham, J. |author5=Scher, E. |author6=Kadavanich, A. |author7=Alivisatos, A. P. |title=Shape control of CdSe nanocrystals|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|date=2000|volume=404|issue=6773|pages=59–61|doi=10.1038/35003535|pmid=10716439 |bibcode=2000Natur.404...59P |s2cid=4390767 }}</ref> Alivisatos reported on techniques used to select the size but vary the shapes of the nanocrystals produced. This was hailed as a major breakthrough in nanocrystal fabrication because rod-shaped semiconductor nanocrystals can be stacked to create nano-sized electronic devices.

The rod-shaped nanocrystal research, coupled with earlier work led by Alivisatos in which it was shown that quantum dots or "qdots"—nanometer-sized crystal dots (spheres a few billionths of a meter in size)—made from semiconductors such as cadmium selenide can emit multiple colors of light depending upon the size of the crystal, opened the door to using nanocrystals as fluorescent probes for the study of biological materials, biomedical research tools and aids to diagnosis,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Alivisatos|first1=P.|title=Less is More in Medicine|journal=Scientific American|volume=17|issue=3|pages=72–79|date=August 17, 2007|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0907-72sp}}</ref> and as light-emitting diodes (LEDs). Alivisatos went on to use his techniques to create an entirely new generation of hybrid solar cells that combined nanotechnology with plastic electronics.<ref name="University of California Berkeley"/>

=== Applications ===
Alivisatos is the founding scientist of Quantum Dot Corporation,<ref>{{cite news|last1=Chang|first1=K.|title=Tiny Is Beautiful: Translating 'Nano' Into Practical|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/02/22/science/22nano.html?pagewanted=print&module=Search&mabReward=relbias%3Ar|access-date=June 9, 2014|work=article|agency=New York Times|date=February 22, 2005}}</ref> a company that makes crystalline nanoscale tags that are used in the study of cell behavior.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Feder|first1=B.J.|title=Bashful vs. Brash in the New Field of Nanotech|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/03/15/business/technology-bashful-vs-brash-in-the-new-field-of-nanotech.html|access-date=June 9, 2014|work=article|agency=New York Times|date=March 15, 2004}}</ref> (Quantum Dot is now part of Life Technologies.) He also founded the nanotechnology company Nanosys,<ref>{{cite news|last1=Kanellos|first1=M.|title=Samsung Invests in Nanosys, Licenses Technology|url=http://www.greentechmedia.com/articles/read/samsung-invests-in-nanosys-licenses-technology|access-date=June 9, 2014|work=article|agency=greentechsolar|publisher=greentechmedia|date=August 10, 2010}}</ref> and Solexant, a photovoltaic start-up that has since restarted as [[Siva Power]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Wesoff|first1=E.|title=Solexant Rebrands as Siva and Looks to Scale CIGS Thin-Film Solar|url=http://www.greentechmedia.com/articles/read/Solexant-Rebrands-as-Siva-and-Looks-to-Scale-CIGS-Thin-Film-Solar|access-date=June 9, 2014|work=article|agency=greentechmedia|date=November 21, 2013}}</ref> His research has led to the development of applications in range of industries, including bioimaging (for example, the use of quantum dots for luminescent labeling of biological tissue); display technologies (his quantum dot emissive film is found in the Kindle Fire HDX tablet);<ref>{{cite news|author1=Chatterjee, S. |author2=Maan, L.|title=With sharp focus, quantum dot makers scale up to meet demand|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/electronics-quantum-dots-idUSL4N0PB2LM20140813|access-date=August 30, 2014|work=article|agency=Reuters|publisher=Thomson Reuters|date=August 13, 2014}}</ref> and renewable energy (solar applications of quantum dots).

=== Editorships ===
Alivisatos is the founding editor of ''[[Nano Letters]]'', a publication of the American Chemical Society.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alivisatos Group People |url=https://www.cchem.berkeley.edu/pagrp/people.html |access-date=October 10, 2016 |website=www.cchem.berkeley.edu}}</ref> He formerly served on the Senior Editorial Board of ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]''. He has also served on the editorial advisory boards of'' [[ACS Nano]]'', the ''[[Journal of Physical Chemistry A|Journal of Physical Chemistry]]'', ''Chemical Physics'', the ''[[Journal of Chemical Physics]]'', and ''[[Advanced Materials]]''.

Paul Alivisatos"|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/a-paul-alivisatos-imuucq/|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|access-date=June 9, 2014}}</ref> the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Book of Members|url=https://www.amacad.org/multimedia/pdfs/publications/bookofmembers/ChapterA.pdf|website=www.amacad.org|publisher=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|access-date=June 10, 2014}}</ref> and the [[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dnva.no/medlemmer/53|title=Utenlandske medlemmer - Den matematisk-naturvitenskapelige klasse|publisher=Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters|language=no|access-date=8 September 2026}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Alivisatos is married to Nicole Alivisatos, a retired chemist, former editor of the journal [[Nano Letters]], and daughter of the noted chemist, [[Gábor A. Somorjai]]. They have two daughters.<ref name="r799">{{cite web | title=Paul Alivisatos life story | website=The Kavli Prize | date=June 4, 2024 | url=https://www.kavliprize.org/paul-alivisatos-autobiography | access-date=September 26, 2025}}</ref>
